generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport the values of academic integrity are not abstract. Honesty means being clear about which findings are yours and which come from the literature, the lab or the field. Trust means a reader can rely on your citations leading to real studies that say what you claim. Responsibility means owning the inferences you draw from a result. The school spans sport and exercise science, coaching, management and therapy, and each weighs its evidence differently, lab data in one, training judgement or participation figures in another. Referencing is where these shared values become visible on the page, whatever the subject.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two sport and exercise science students writing up an idea they first met in a physiology seminar reading.

Tom likes the idea, rephrases it, and builds a paragraph around it without naming where it came from. Nothing is copied word for word, so it feels safe. But the reader is left to assume the thinking is Tom's own. The omission is not a formatting slip; it quietly breaks the honesty and trust that writing in sport science depends on.

Amara uses the same idea but attributes it to the researcher who proposed it, then adds a line of her own about what the finding does and does not establish. The reference is not defensive cover; it is Amara being honest about the debt, respectful of the researcher, and responsible for the further claim. The paragraph is stronger for it, because the reader can see exactly where Amara's own contribution begins.

Both students used the idea well. Only Amara treated referencing as an expression of the values, rather than a rule to be managed.
generatedProse.summary: Academic integrity in the School of Sport is best understood not as a rulebook but as a set of shared values: honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and courage. Referencing is one visible expression of those values rather than a hoop to clear, whether your evidence is lab data, a training session or a participation survey. You can now articulate what integrity means, explain how a value shows up in real sport work, and appraise a difficult situation against the values. The next lesson turns to why referencing in particular matters so much.

check.body: In the worked example, what was the real problem with Tom's paragraph?

items.text: By not attributing the idea, he let the reader assume borrowed thinking was his own, breaking honesty and trust.
He rephrased the idea instead of quoting it directly.
He used an idea from a seminar reading rather than from a journal.
He added a line of his own about what the finding established.

feedback.correct: That's right. The breach was in letting borrowed thinking pass as his own, which is where honesty and trust give way.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the reader was left to assume, and which values that affects.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The problem was that the idea went unattributed, so the reader assumed the thinking was Tom's own. That breaks honesty and trust, whatever the formatting looks like.
